t: Introduction: physical factors and forensic medical significance
n: In this topic four groups of physical factors are considered: high and low temperature, electric current, changes in pressure, and radiation. Although electrical injury accounts for 1-2.5% of all injuries, it occupies one of the leading places in disability and mortality. Barotrauma, that is, injury from a change in pressure, is rare in forensic medical examination practice. Radiation injury is also relatively rare. Except for nuclear explosions, in all cases it results from an accident.

t: Body temperature and routes of heat loss
n: Body temperature and routes of heat loss. Normal body temperature is 36-37°C; it is maintained by regulation of heat production and heat loss. Heat is lost mainly by radiation, which is 55 %; by sweat 27 %, by conduction 15 %, with various excretions 3 %. A temperature below 22-25°C or above 43-44°C produces changes in the tissues incompatible with life. General action leads to heat stroke or hypothermia, local action to a burn or frostbite.

t: Heat stroke: conditions and predisposing factors
n: Heat stroke: conditions and predisposing factors. Heat stroke arises when much heat is produced in the body and little is lost. Conditions: high air temperature and humidity, absence of wind; hot workshops, heavy physical work, training of athletes and military personnel. Clothing impermeable to air and moisture, cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, obesity and old age predispose. In children under one year the mechanisms of thermoregulation are not fully formed, so they are very sensitive to high temperature.

t: Heat stroke: mechanism of development
n: Heat stroke: mechanism of development. First, much heat is produced and little is lost. Impairment of haemodynamics takes the main place: the blood thickens and circulation slows. This state intensifies tissue hyperthermia and leads to tissue hypoxia. In the stress reaction catecholamines and glucocorticoids are released, stasis is seen in the microcirculation, and as a result a metabolic disturbance develops. That is, the process begins with heat and passes to disturbances of circulation and at the tissue level.

t: Acute and protracted forms of heat stroke
n: Forms of heat stroke. In the acute form consciousness is suddenly lost, coma occurs and death follows within a short time from cardiac and respiratory failure. The protracted form develops slowly and is divided into three periods: first CNS activity is depressed, then comes a period of excitation, with restlessness, headache and tachycardia. The third is the period of weakness: temperature above 41-42°C, coma and convulsions. The period of weakness is considered preagonal. When body temperature exceeds 42-43°C, death occurs from primary cessation of breathing.

t: Sunstroke (insolation)
n: Sunstroke, that is, insolation. It arises when sunlight acts on the head for a long time in an open place without a head covering. Heating of the head impairs the activity of the central nervous system: headache, clouding of consciousness, excitation, hallucinations and convulsions are seen. First the pulse and breathing quicken, then the pulse slows. Pathological breathing and paralysis of the respiratory centre may occur. Attention: unlike heat stroke, a significant rise in body temperature is not characteristic. There may be a first-degree burn on the skin, that is, erythema.

t: Changes in the body in heat stroke and sunstroke
n: Changes in the body in heat stroke and sunstroke. In bodies of those who died of heat stroke and sunstroke, the morphological changes are similar. In neither is there a specific sign. The brain and its membranes are sharply congested and oedematous, with small perivascular haemorrhages in the brain. There is thick blood in the heart chambers and large vessels. Mucus accumulates in the airways, and the lungs take on a brown tint because of the thick blood. Rigor mortis develops rapidly and is strong, whereas cadaveric lividity appears late and in small amount. The internal organs are congested, and small haemorrhages are found beneath the serous membranes.

t: Case analysis: a body found in a hot workshop
n: Case analysis: a body found in a hot workshop. Situation: an obese worker in clothing impermeable to air died after heavy physical work in a hot workshop. These conditions create a predisposition to heat stroke. In the body the brain is congested and oedematous, the heart contains thick blood, rigor is rapid and strong, lividity late and scanty; these findings are consistent with heat stroke. Question: can heat stroke be categorically proved from these findings alone, and why is it necessary to study the circumstances of the event? Direction of the answer: morphology is not specific, so the circumstances of the event and the conditions are assessed. If they are not attended to, an erroneous clinical diagnosis may be made.

t: Quick question: heat stroke and sunstroke
n: Quick question: heat stroke and sunstroke. First question: does body temperature rise significantly in sunstroke? Answer: no, a significant rise in temperature is not characteristic of this state. Second question: what three periods are there in the protracted form of heat stroke? Answer: the periods of depression of the CNS, that is, central nervous system, excitation and weakness. Third question: from what does death occur when body temperature exceeds 42-43°C? Answer: from primary cessation of breathing. Attention: because of the absence of specific clinical signs and inattention to the history, an erroneous clinical diagnosis is sometimes made.

t: Thermal burn: causes and importance of area
n: Thermal burn: causes and importance of area. In local action, a thermal burn arises if the temperature of the skin and underlying tissues exceeds 45-50°C. The nature of the burn depends on the type of source, its temperature and duration of action, and on the affected region. Sources: flame, tar, napalm, bitumen, water hotter than 60°C, scalding steam, gases and a heated object. Where the skin is thin the burn is deeper. In forensic medical assessment, besides the degree of the burn, the area of the injury is also important.

t: Degrees of thermal burn
n: Degrees of thermal burn. Degrees I and II are regarded as superficial, degrees III and IV as deep burns. In most cases different degrees occur together in one injury, for example II-III. In degree I there is redness and swelling, which pass without trace in 3-4 days. In degree II serous blisters appear and heal in 10-20 days without a scar. In degree III there is necrosis: III-A superficial, III-B full thickness; granulation begins in 2-3 weeks. In degree IV necrosis of muscle, ligaments and bone is seen. Attention: degree IV occurs only from the action of flame; degrees I-III arise from any source.

t: Identifying the heat source: liquid, flame, heated object
n: Identifying the heat source. From the features of the burn the type of source of high temperature can be determined. With hot liquid the hair and clothing are not damaged, the burn is superficial, and the runs are directed downward; the liquid may seep under clothing and footwear and burn covered areas. With flame the hair and clothing are damaged, the burn is tongue-shaped and deep, and there are traces of soot. With a heated object the burn is deep, the surface limited, and the shape matches the contact surface. The site of the wounds shows the position at the time of the event: runs are directed downward, "tongues of flame" upward.

t: Rules for assessing burn area
n: Rules for assessing burn area. The rule of nines, A. Wallace, 1951, allows the burn area to be determined approximately. According to it, head and neck are 9 %, each arm 9 %, the front of the trunk 18 %, the back 18 %, the perineum 1 %. Palm rule: the surface of the palm makes up about 1% of the total body surface. Dangerous to life: a burn of more than 10% of the body of degree III-IV, more than 15% of degree III, more than 20% of degree II. This means that, besides the degree, the area also determines the prognosis.

t: Writing the burn diagnosis and danger to life
n: Writing the burn diagnosis and danger to life. In the diagnosis the burn is written as a fraction: in the numerator the burn area, in the denominator the degrees of burn. The degree and area are stated as fully as possible. Examples: 10 % / II or 30% (10%) / II-III. In brackets the area of the deeper burn is given. A burn of the airways, accompanied by oedema of the airways and narrowing of the glottis, is regarded as dangerous to life. If burn disease develops, thermal burns of smaller area are also life-threatening.

t: Burn disease and its periods
n: Burn disease and its periods. Burn disease consists of four periods. The first is burn shock, up to 1 day. The second is toxaemia, 1-2 weeks. The third is septicotoxaemia, 2-3 weeks. The fourth is convalescence, that is, the period of recovery. If an airway burn and carbon monoxide are added, the probability of death increases two-fold or more. In septicotoxaemia purulent complications occur: pneumonia, abscess, phlegmon, pyelonephritis, sepsis. In children the disease is more severe; in the elderly it is aggravated by concomitant diseases.

t: Establishing vitality of the action of flame
n: Establishing vitality of the action of flame. If there is soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life. Soot is also sought in the cavities of the skull and in the vessels. Carboxyhaemoglobin is determined in the blood of the heart chambers and deep vessels: in action during life up to 60%, and in postmortem action it does not exceed 20%. Carboxymyoglobin is examined in deep-lying muscles. Remember: in postmortem action of flame carboxyhaemoglobin may also be found in the blood of superficial vessels.

t: Other signs of vitality
n: Other signs of vitality. In action during life the eyeballs are usually not damaged. When the eyelid skin is stretched, burnt and unburnt areas alternate, this is the "crow's foot". A burn of the airways, many blood clots in the heart and vessels, arterial thrombi and fat embolism of the pulmonary vessels indicate life. The protein content in blisters formed during life is twice that in blisters formed after death. An epidural haematoma from trauma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura mater. One from postmortem action of flame is crescent-shaped and not attached.

t: Burnt body: pugilistic posture and time of burning
n: Burnt body: pugilistic posture and time of burning. Under the action of flame moisture evaporates, and because of protein coagulation the muscles become dense and shorten. The limbs flex, forming the "pugilistic posture". The skin coverings also become dense; if different parts of the body are exposed unequally, cracks and splits may form in the skin. Bodies of infants burn to ash in 2-3 hours. Those of adults take about 20 hours, and in a gas crematorium less than an hour. To resolve questions of species, sex, age and others, the ash remaining from a burnt body may be examined forensically.

t: Case analysis: a body found after a fire
n: Case analysis: a body found after a fire. Situation: after a fire a charred body was found, the limbs flexed in the "pugilistic posture". Question: did death occur before the action of flame? If there is soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life; soot may also be found in the vessels and in liver cells. In postmortem action of flame carboxyhaemoglobin does not exceed 20%, in action during life it reaches 60%; blood is taken from the heart chambers and deep vessels. Attention: a traumatic epidural haematoma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura mater, a postmortem one crescent-shaped and not attached.

t: General action of low temperature: factors
n: General action of low temperature: factors. High humidity, strong wind, clothing unsuited to the season, immobility and fatigue create a predisposition to hypothermia. Alcohol dilates the skin vessels and increases heat loss; an intoxicated person misjudges the situation and takes no protective measures. Newborns are very sensitive: thermoregulation is not fully formed, and the body surface is large relative to mass. In cold water death may occur in 1-1.5 hours. Prolonged exposure even at an air temperature up to +10°C may lead to hypothermia.

t: Hypothermia: stages of pathogenesis
n: Hypothermia: stages of pathogenesis. The first stage is compensation: at first metabolism increases, glycogen decreases, skin vessels constrict and heat loss decreases. The second is decompensation, temperature falls. In the third, at +30…+28°C, the cortex is impaired. The fourth is the final stage, +25…+22°C. The fifth is death: cessation of breathing or collapse. When temperature falls by 1°C, biochemical processes in the tissues slow about 2-fold. Death most often occurs from cessation of breathing, sometimes from vascular collapse or ventricular fibrillation.

t: External signs in hypothermia
n: External signs in hypothermia. In the posture of a person who has frozen, the arms are flexed to the chest and the legs to the abdomen; the heat-losing surface is reduced. Raisky's sign: ice around the mouth and nose, rime on the eyebrows and eyelashes. Puparev's sign: the testis is contracted and the scrotum drawn up. Cadaveric lividity at below-zero temperature is pinkish-red, at above-zero temperature up to +10°C it may be bluish-violet. Attention: in severe intoxication the posture may be absent; and a layer of ice beneath the snow is not a specific sign.

t: Internal signs in hypothermia
n: Internal signs in hypothermia. The internal organs are congested and all tissues are pinkish-red. Because death comes slowly, clotted bright scarlet blood is found in the left chambers of the heart, the aorta and large arteries. Pukhnarevich's sign: the stomach is empty and considerably smaller in size. Fabrikantov's sign: because of increased permeability of the vascular wall, there are diapedetic haemorrhages in the internal organs, including the mucosa of the renal pelves.

t: Vishnevsky spots
n: Vishnevsky spots. They are found in the stomach, sometimes on the tops of the duodenal folds, up to 0.5 cm in size; they are washed off by a stream of water. Chain of formation: low temperature acts, the autonomic nervous system is disturbed, spasm and diapedesis of erythrocytes are seen, and haemorrhagic infarction and necrosis appear. Hydrochloric acid converts haemoglobin to acid haematin, so the colour changes from red to brown. The spots occur in 80-90% of deaths from hypothermia; in rapid death and often in children they are few or absent.

t: Micro- and histochemical signs of hypothermia
n: Micro- and histochemical signs of hypothermia. Under the microscope spasm of the microcirculatory bed, oedema of the organ stroma and small haemorrhages are seen. On histochemistry, glycogen disappears from the liver, pancreas, heart and brain. In the adrenal cortex lipoids decrease. In the straight tubules of the kidney there are necrobiotic changes, this is Kasyanov's sign. Attention: if death occurred in a short time, in ice-cold water and wind, blood sugar decreases or disappears, but glycogen may be preserved in the liver. In severe intoxication blood alcohol may be low and urine alcohol high; the reason is strong utilisation of alcohol in the body.

t: Freezing of the body and thawing
n: Freezing of the body and thawing. After death at below-zero temperature the body may freeze regardless of the cause. The injuries that form must be distinguished from injuries inflicted during life. On freezing the volume of the brain and parenchymatous organs increases. Fractures of the skull bones and separation of the sutures are possible; this is seen when the neck freezes before the head. A frozen body is usually thawed at room temperature, which may take several days. To shorten the time, warm air or hot water, up to +50°C, is used. On thawing, erythrocytes undergo haemolysis; the faster the thawing, the stronger the haemolysis of blood and postmortem imbibition of the tissues.

t: Case analysis: a body found in winter
n: Case analysis: a body found in winter. A hypothetical situation: in winter, at below-zero temperature, a body was found outdoors. The arms are flexed to the chest, the legs to the abdomen, and there is rime on the eyebrows and eyelashes. On internal examination the stomach is empty and reduced; on the tops of the mucosal folds there are small haemorrhages up to 0.5 cm in diameter. Question: what are these signs called after their authors, and why is the cadaveric lividity pinkish-red? Attention: a layer of ice beneath the snow is not a specific sign. In severe intoxication the posture may be absent, and alcohol may be low in blood and high in urine.

t: Local action of low temperature: frostbite
n: Local action of low temperature: frostbite. In local frostbite body temperature as a whole is normal and falls only in individual areas. Often it is an accident: on the tips of the limbs, ears, nose and cheeks. Mechanism: spasm of the blood vessels, then paralysis; circulation slows or stops, and tissue nutrition is impaired. The latent period is the fall in temperature during the cold exposure. The reactive period begins after the area warms up; the degree is determined in this period. Repercussion: if one hand is frostbitten, changes may appear on the opposite hand too. Dangerous to life: more than 10% of degree III-IV, more than 15% of degree III, more than 20% of degree II.

t: Degrees of frostbite
n: Degrees of frostbite. In degree I there is a reddish-bluish tint, which passes in 3-7 days. In degree II a clear blister forms, lasting 10-20 days. In degree III there is skin necrosis, 1-2 months and a scar remains. In degree IV there is necrosis down to the bone, lasting weeks or months. In degrees I-II no scar remains, but the area stays very sensitive to cold for a long time. In degree III demarcation inflammation develops, often with suppuration. In degree IV the demarcation rim forms at the end of the second week; it is often complicated by purulent infection.

t: Electric current: properties and groups of factors
n: Electric current: properties and groups of factors. Electrical injury accounts for 1-2.5% of all injuries, but is one of the leaders in disability and mortality. Current cannot be detected without instruments; it acts by contact, through another object or at a distance. The energy of the current is converted into thermal, chemical and mechanical forms; even in short exposure the injury may be severe. The factors are divided into three groups. The first is the properties of the current: type, voltage, strength, frequency. The second is the organism: age, illness, intoxication, skin resistance. The third is interaction: duration, connection and path of the current.

t: Current type, voltage, strength and frequency
n: Current type, voltage, strength and frequency. Up to 500 volts alternating current is more dangerous, and above 500 volts direct current is more dangerous. The safe voltage norm is 24 volts. Most deaths occur from current of 220–380 volts. A current of 50 mA threatens life, and at 100 mA death is frequently seen. The most dangerous frequency is 40–60 hertz. Current of 10000 hertz and above does no harm and is used in physiotherapy.

t: Factors of the organism and of the conditions of connection
n: Factors of the organism and of the conditions of connection. Current passes through tissues of low resistance, that is, blood, mucous membranes and liver. The greatest resistance is in bone and skin, and the changes are also found there. Moist skin, sweating, damp clothing and metal ornaments reduce resistance; for this reason death is commoner in summer. In prolonged exposure: at 10–15 milliamperes the muscles contract involuntarily, from 25 milliamperes respiratory convulsion, from 80 milliamperes fibrillation. It is dangerous if the current passes through the heart and brain. Step voltage is the potential difference across a step of 0.8 m; do not approach a broken wire closer than 10 m.

t: Specific and non-specific action of electric current
n: Specific and non-specific action of electric current. In general action the electrical processes of the cells are disrupted: ventricular fibrillation of the heart, respiratory disturbance and electrogenic shock develop. Electrogenic asphyxia arises when the current passes through the brain, because of clonic convulsion of the respiratory muscles and spasm of the glottis. Chemical action: coagulative necrosis at the anode, colliquative necrosis at the cathode. Thermal action: burn and "pearl beads" of 1–5 mm in the bone. Mechanical action: dislocation of joints and fractures of bones. Non-specific action: ignition of clothing, burn of the eyes, falling during convulsions.

t: Electric mark and electrical burn
n: Electric mark and electrical burn. The electric mark is round or oval, firm on palpation. The edge is raised and the centre depressed in the form of a crater. The temperature is up to 120°C, and thermal action is the leading one. In electrical burn the temperature is above 120°C, thermal and chemical action together, with necrosis of all layers and charring. Metallisation gives colouring: copper bluish-green, iron yellow-black; the metal of the conductor is detected by X-ray and spectrography. Under the microscope cavities and palisade-like cells are seen in the epidermis. The complication is electrogenic oedema and necrosis.

t: Types of death in electrical injury and apparent death
n: Types of death in electrical injury and apparent death, according to Avdeev. The first is superfast death, from primary cardiac and respiratory arrest. The second is slow death: at first there are signs of life such as convulsions and screaming. The third is interrupted death: it occurs after release and recovery of consciousness. The fourth is late death: after hours to a day, from an early complication. Apparent death, vita minima, in which the vital centres are inhibited. Resuscitation is carried out until a cadaveric spot appears.

t: Action of lightning
n: Action of lightning. Lightning is a gigantic atmospheric discharge: the voltage is millions of volts, and the current reaches hundreds of thousands of amperes. The duration is ten-thousandths of a second. Damaging factors: electric current, light, sound and the shock wave. The action is direct or indirect, through a telephone, television or radio. Burns and marks resembling an electric mark appear on the skin. Although the outer clothing may be intact, the underclothing may be damaged; metal objects melt. The "lightning figure" is a red-pink tree-like pattern on the skin. It disappears after hours or a day, so it is photographed immediately.

t: Barotrauma: action of high pressure
n: Barotrauma: action of high pressure. As depth increases, hydrostatic pressure rises: at 10 m it is twice, at 20 m three times atmospheric pressure. If pressure in the lungs changes abruptly by 80–100 mm Hg, barotrauma occurs: alveolar rupture, pneumothorax, haemorrhage. Chain of pulmonary barotrauma: rapid ascent in scuba gear, sharp rise of intrapulmonary pressure, rupture of lung tissue, passage of air into the left heart and blood, embolism of the cerebral arteries. In a diver, squeeze of the body: the head enlarges, the face turns blue and swells, and there are small haemorrhages in the eyes.

t: Gas poisoning and decompression sickness
n: Gas poisoning and decompression sickness. In poisoning by oxygen and carbon dioxide no specific morphological change is found in the body. The diagnosis rests on the circumstances of death, the clinical picture and absence of other causes of death. With oxygen there are hyperoxaemia and enzyme inactivation, and neurotoxic and pulmonary forms occur. If the concentration of carbon dioxide is 3% or more, dyspnoea, headache and sweating appear. Nitrogen is highly soluble in fat, the brain is sensitive, and intoxication resembling alcoholic intoxication and euphoria appear. On rapid ascent, nitrogen bubbles cause gas embolism and caisson disease; in it clots with gas bubbles are found in the right heart and veins, and subcutaneous emphysema.

t: Low pressure, radiation and conclusion
n: Low pressure, radiation and conclusion. In altitude sickness oxygen is insufficient, and the cardiovascular and respiratory systems are impaired first; at 18000 m, at 6 kPa, tissue fluids "boil". Forms of radiation sickness by dose: up to 10 gray bone marrow, 10–20 intestinal, 20–80 toxaemic, above 80 cerebral. The bone marrow form at a dose above 6 gray leads to death. In acute radiation sickness there are a primary reaction, a latent period, 2–4 weeks, and a period of marked clinical signs. Death is often at the end of week 4 from an infectious complication. The examination decides: the type of damaging factor, the physical properties of the source, the dose, the number and time of exposures, and the severity of bodily harm.
